NEPA Insights Fact Sheet

Key Points and Policy Implications

Published

March 18, 2026

Download PDF version

Executive Summary

Key Findings
  • There are diminishing returns to broad NEPA reform for decarbonization since they are not likely to require major federal review (EA or EIS). Most decarbonization projects in this corpus use Categorical Exclusions: 93.6% for decarbonization projects overall, versus 85.2% for fossil energy and 85.9% for other project types.
  • There are real efficiency gains to be had in agency-level implementation. Programmatic and tiered reviews remain rare (161 of 1,326 decarbonization EA/EIS reviews; 12.1%), but tiered EISs are faster on median than standard and programmatic EISs (593, 1087, and 914 days, respectively).
  • Permitting reforms in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 have had a real, but modest, impact. Post-FRA, 30% of EAs still exceed the 75-page limit; for EISs, 43% exceed 300 pages and another 29% fall between 151 and 300 pages.

1. There Are Diminishing Returns to NEPA Reform for Speeding Decarbonization Projects

How are these as alternative, catchier options for this first point?


  • The dirty secret of NEPA reform: it mostly helps the wrong projects: the vast majority of decarbonization-related projects never require environmental assessment or environmental impact statements

  • Streamlining NEPA won’t supercharge the clean energy transition—the vast majority of decarbonization-related projects never require environmental assessment or environmental impact statements.

Decarbonization projects use categorical exclusions at higher rates than fossil fuel or other project types; fossil fuel projects have higher EA/EIS rates than decarbonization projects. Across 20,725 decarbonization actions, 93.6% use Categorical Exclusions. That is materially higher than the CE share for fossil projects (85.2%) and for the residual “other” category (85.9%). That means reforms aimed only at accelerating EAs and EISs will affect only a limited slice of the decarbonization pipeline.

Only DOE and BLM have complete CE, EA, and EIS coverage in NEPATEC 2.0 — and both confirm that decarbonization actions are heavily concentrated in lower-intensity review pathways. In the strongest-coverage portion of the dataset, DOE records show 98.0% of actions as CEs. BLM, the only other agency with full coverage, shows a more balanced mix but remains heavily CE-weighted. That does not mean DOE or BLM should be treated as representative of every federal agency. It does mean that, even where the underlying CE/EA/EIS coverage is comparatively good, the decarbonization portfolio is still overwhelmingly concentrated in the lowest-intensity NEPA pathway.

NEPA is just not really a problem for solar. Within the current technology-tagged output, there are 2,483 solar actions total; 91.7% are CEs and only 4.8% are EISs. Within this federal-review corpus, NEPA is therefore not the main bottleneck for most solar activity. Other constraints such as transmission access, interconnection, land availability, agency capacity, and financing may matter more often than full-scale NEPA review.

Coverage Caveat

NEPATEC 2.0 is a corpus of federal environmental review documents, not a census of all U.S. decarbonization activity. Agency comparisons also need care: EIS coverage is government-wide, but EA/CE coverage is complete only for DOE and BLM — all other agencies are represented primarily via the EPA EIS database and therefore appear with inflated EIS shares.

2. There Are Real Efficiency Gains to Be Had in NEPA Implementation at the Agency Level

Programmatic and tiered reviews: The evidence on programmatic and tiered reviews indicates that there are real efficiency gains from avoiding project-specific environmental impact statements. However, programmatic and tiered reviews are rare: only 161 of 1,326 decarbonization EA/EIS reviews (12.1%) are programmatic or tiered.

Tiered EAs take longer than standard EAs on median (734 versus 421 days), but they are still much shorter than a full EIS. The more important efficiency gain appears to be at the EIS level: tiered EISs have a median duration of 593 days, compared with 1087 days for standard EISs and 914 days for programmatic EISs. The practical lesson is that tiering helps most when it allows an agency to avoid repeating full project-specific EIS analysis, not when it is expected to marginally speed up an EA.

Interagency coordination: Previous CATF research on transmission permitting has demonstrated that insufficient support for agency coordination, cooperation, and capacity contributes to longer permitting timelines. This research builds on that finding by mapping which agencies collaborate the most on NEPA reviews. In the current output tables, DOE stands out as the clear hub of the multi-department network, with a bridge score of 32 compared with 11.3 for DOI. That suggests that improving DOE-DOI collaboration through targeted staffing increases, memoranda of understanding, and other mechanisms may have outsized impact on review timelines.

This is consistent with the broader permitting literature: bottlenecks often arise not from NEPA’s existence as a statute, but from uneven agency capacity, fragmented authority, and weak coordination routines. Those are implementation problems, and they can be addressed without reopening the statute itself.

3. Permitting Reforms in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 Have Had a Real, but Modest, Impact

The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (Public Law 118-5) introduced page limits for NEPA environmental reviews. Under the law, environmental impact statements must be 150 pages or less, or 300 pages or less for proposals of extraordinary complexity, and environmental assessments must be 75 pages or less.

The Phase 1 analysis finds a real but modest post-FRA shift in document length. Average and median regulatory page counts decline after the FRA threshold, which is consistent with agencies responding to the new statutory limits. At the same time, the post-FRA sample is still small: only 33 EAs and 42 EISs are in the current compliance table.

The page limits had an effect, though the evidence is not yet definitive. 30% of post-FRA EAs still exceed the 75-page limit. For EISs, 43% exceed even the 300-page ceiling, while another 29% fall in the 151–300 page range and may still be defensible under the “extraordinary complexity” exception. The practical conclusion is that the FRA has changed incentives, but not yet produced consistent compliance.

This ambiguity is unsurprising. Many post-FRA decisions were likely already well underway when the law took effect, creating a transitional cohort in which agencies had to balance page-limit pressure against other statutory timing and process requirements. A fuller assessment will require more decisions from projects initiated after June 3, 2023.

Caveats and Considerations

Several considerations from the fact sheet should remain front-of-mind when translating these findings into policy recommendations.

  • Data quality and completeness remain a structural limitation. Better federal metadata standards and document-linkage practices would improve nearly every downstream permitting analysis. Existing efforts such as PermitAI, CEQ’s NEPA data standard, and the ePermit Act move in the right direction, but they do not yet solve the broader fragmentation problem.
  • High CE usage is not automatically a normative success. Streamlined review can be appropriate, but faster timelines do not always imply better environmental analysis or better public decision-making.
  • Shorter timelines are not the only policy goal. Review quality, legal durability, agency learning, and public legitimacy matter alongside speed.
  • Some of the most important questions remain outside this Phase 1 scope. In particular, the present work does not directly test whether NEPA was the actual cause of project delay, nor does it comprehensively analyze when agencies may have relied on CEs too aggressively.

Taken together, the Phase 1 evidence suggests a fairly specific policy posture: be skeptical of claims that broad NEPA reform will dramatically accelerate decarbonization on its own; focus instead on agency capacity, coordination, data systems, and targeted use of programmatic tools where those changes can plausibly alter outcomes.
